name: Tourism & Hospitality
label: SECTOR EXPLORATION PACK | WORKSHOP 1
referenceMarket: United States (Miami/Florida as a reference case; national-scope ideas are welcome)
intro: This Pack gives you a common starting point: vocabulary, structure and verified figures. It does not define the problem, customer or solution. That is your job.
definition: Businesses that move, host, entertain and serve people traveling away from home for leisure, business or events, plus the technology and services that power them.
inside: B2B technology and services serving all of the above (software, payments, data, staffing)
outside: Independent restaurants with no tourism link

players.howMoney: Owns or operates the asset: room revenue, food & beverage, on-board spend, spa, ancillary fees. High fixed costs, seasonal demand.
players.examples: Hotels and resorts (Fontainebleau Miami Beach, The Biltmore), Carnival, Royal Caribbean

players.howMoney: Franchise and management fees (% of revenue or profit), loyalty programs and co-branded cards. Owners carry the real estate.
Commission or take rate per booking; advertising and pay-per-click from suppliers.
Two-sided marketplace: service fees charged to guests and/or hosts per stay.

players.type: Experience marketplaces, tour operators and DMCs
players.howMoney: Commission on bookings, markup on packages, supplier fees. Destination management companies sell local ground services to groups and brands.
players.examples: Viator, GetYourGuide, Fever, Klook, local tour operators

players.howMoney: Service fees and supplier commissions; subscription or transaction fees in managed business travel.
Per-ticket service fees, dynamic pricing, software subscriptions for organizers, sponsorship.
SaaS subscription (per room, per user), payment and transaction fees, usage-based pricing. Includes property management, booking engines, POS, revenue management, channel managers and distribution.
players.examples: Cloudbeds, Mews, Oracle Opera, Toast, Sabre, Amadeus, FareHarbor

playersNote: Illustrative map, not exhaustive. Examples are well-known players to help you recognize each model, not a recommendation to copy them.

valueChain.note: One possible lens. The chain changes by segment (cruise, events, rentals, B2B software). Map the one that fits your area of interest and decide where value is created and captured.

keyFigures.figure: $1.35 trillion total travel spending in 2025; domestic travelers account for $1.2 trillion (87%) across about 2.4 billion domestic trips
15 million jobs supported by travel; $3.0 trillion in total economic output
68.3 million international arrivals in 2025 vs. 72.4 million in 2024; NTTO projects about 70.5 million in 2026
International visitors spend about $173 billion (2025 estimate), the largest U.S. services export; overseas visitors can spend up to 8x more per trip than domestic travelers
37.2 million cruise passengers worldwide in 2025, of which 20.6 million sourced from the U.S.; the Caribbean is about 43% of global deployments
keyFigures.source: CLIA, State of the Cruise Industry 2026

keyFigures.figure: 143.3 million visitors in 2025 (preliminary): 131.1M domestic, 9.3M overseas, 2.9M Canadian. Brazil is now the #2 international source
28.3 million visitors and $22.7 billion in visitor spending in 2025 (+4.1% vs. 2024); $32.2 billion total economic impact
216,000+ tourism jobs (about 10% of county employment); lodging is $10.4 billion, nearly half of visitor spending
International visitors spend over $1,150 per person per trip. Top markets: Colombia, Brazil, UK, Canada, Mexico, Argentina, Spain, Italy, Germany, France
Passed 10 million cruise passengers in fiscal year 2026 (Oct. 2025 to Sep. 2026), above the prior record of 8.56 million

figuresNote: Some figures are preliminary or estimates. Always check the latest release and cite the source and year in your own work.
challenge: Travel and hospitality is one of the largest consumer and business sectors in the U.S., yet demand is shifting between domestic and international travelers, and incumbents, platforms and software providers all compete for the same traveler dollar. Identify one specific, evidence-backed friction experienced by a clearly defined customer (a traveler, an operator or a business) in this sector in the U.S., and show why it is worth solving now. Choose an initial launch market (for example Miami/Florida or another U.S. region) and justify your choice with data.
pestelNote: Sprint 1, PESTEL: each team member takes one dimension. The figures above are a starting point only; look for what is changing and who it affects.

sprint2Questions.question: Which types of companies capture most of the value in your segment, and who is entering or leaving?
At which step of the chain do travelers or operators lose time, money or trust? Who captures the margin?
What do people still do manually, or work around, today? What evidence shows it matters (data, reviews, reports)?
How is the problem solved today, and by whom? What do those solutions fail to do?
Which customer is most affected: leisure, business, international, domestic, local operator? How big is that group?
Which revenue model fits your idea (commission, subscription, SaaS, fees)? Who pays, and why?

glossary.def: Average Daily Rate: average room revenue per occupied room
Share of available rooms sold in a period
Share of a transaction a platform keeps as revenue
Destination management company: local ground services for groups
Property management system: hotel core software (reservations, billing)
Global distribution system linking suppliers with travel sellers
Customer acquisition cost / lifetime value of a customer
Predictable swings in demand across the year
